name: Olga Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I tend the feeder belt at a large limestone mine, keeping the rock moving into the crusher and clearing a jam only after the line is locked off. I came here two years ago after the laundry closed, so I'm still junior and ask the old hands before changing a setting. I left school after secondary classes and have no certificate for this machine yet. My husband Peter does a few days of building maintenance when work comes, and our grown children have their own bills. We're trying to make it to retirement, but we have less than a month's expenses saved. I have never used an AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a computer filling forms won't change the belt, so let us get on with the shift. The feeder still needs a person to see where wet rock clumps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the card says pay carries on, but our hours already change with orders and Peter's maintenance days are irregular. I cannot call that safe when our cupboard money runs low before the next wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my feeder checks and ask the shift lead to show me the lock-off procedure again. In the first year I'll put a small fixed amount from every wage into an emergency envelope if the shifts stay long enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried about the ordinary bills, not particularly about this little bit of AI. A late wage can make the whole week feel unsteady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a normal feeder problem look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a sticky load bridged over the feeder and the belt ran empty underneath. I stopped it and called for help rather than reach in while it moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could help with a short week at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Peter we should hold off replacing the sitting-room chairs. Our daughter pays her own rent, so I would not ask her to cover our grocery money.

say: I would say **forms may change**, but the wet rock still needs watching at the feeder.
I would ask to **keep the shift** moving with the same safe lock-off checks.
think: I already fear **variable hours** and Peter’s uncertain maintenance days.
I cannot feel secure with **less than one month** saved, even when AI changes little.
do: **Keep checking** the feeder and review lock-off steps with the shift lead.
**Set aside money** from each wage if enough shifts arrive during the first year.
feel: **Worried** about ordinary bills and thin savings, more than the small AI change.
S0.quote: The feeder still needs a person to see where wet rock clumps.
fieldNote: Her **baseline worry** is irregular household income and almost no savings, even in a plateau.
She describes a real **feeder jam** and safe stop; her small savings plan depends on enough shifts.

steps.text: Keep checking the feeder and reviewing lock-off steps
Put a fixed amount from each wage in an emergency envelope if shifts hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the planning office may use software, but a machine cannot clear my belt yet. I would ask the lead to keep telling us when the delivery schedule changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think new planning could mean fewer hours when the trucks are timed more tightly. There aren't many mine jobs nearby, and I'm the newest operator on this shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for the weekly truck schedule on paper and keep a note of cancelled feeder hours. In the first year I'll cut the paid television service if my shifts fall and ask Peter to help compare the bills on Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel tight in the chest when I picture losing even one regular shift. I know robots are slower in this card, but the schedule can still take money from us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cost would change if a shift disappears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a new delivery plan leaves the feeder idle on Thursday, I lose a day's wage. A lost feeder shift costs a day of wages I was counting on. I would ask the lead whether another line needs a hand before going home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask family to cover the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son that I'm keeping the job while it is there. I would not ask him to send money while he is paying for his own children.

say: I would say **planning software** can change deliveries before robots clear the feeder.
I would ask the lead for **clear schedules** so operators know when work is available.
think: I could lose **feeder hours** if trucks are timed more tightly.
I have **few nearby jobs** and less standing than longer-serving operators.
do: **Request paper schedules** and record cancelled feeder hours during the first year.
**Cancel paid television** if shifts fall, then check the bills with Peter each Sunday.
feel: **Anxious** about losing one regular shift from a thin household budget.
S1.quote: A lost feeder shift costs a day of wages I was counting on.
fieldNote: She connects **thinking-task planning** with her own hours, without claiming capable robots already clear the belt.
Her **first cut** is paid television if shifts fall; she refuses to make grown children carry the shortfall.

steps.text: Keep feeder shifts and record cancellations from the paper schedule
Cancel paid television if feeder shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 may change schedules, while capable robots that clear the feeder arrive around 2031. That is not long when you're nearly sixty and still learning the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the mine could stop giving the newest operator shifts before a robot even arrives. Peter cannot cover our rent and food on his uneven maintenance days, and I cannot pay for another course from an empty envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'll ask the shift lead for a written record of my machine hours and the retirement desk for my contribution statement. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll ask for any paid belt-inspection training, but I'll stay on the feeder unless an actual place and wage are offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because losing even half my hours would put food and heating against each other. I have a list of people to ask, but no money to buy time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your husband if hours fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Peter the truth over supper: we may need to stop sending birthday money to the grandchildren. I hate saying it, but their parents would understand before an unpaid bill arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take inspection training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the lead whether the mine pays people to inspect belts after robots are fitted. If the job exists and they train me on wages, I would take that course; I cannot leave mine work for an unpaid classroom.

say: I would say **2028 thinking AI** may change shifts before capable feeder robots arrive around 2031.
I would ask for **paid belt training** tied to a real job, not an unpaid promise.
think: I may lose **shifts first** as the newest operator, before any robot reaches the feeder.
I think Peter’s uneven income and our **empty cushion** cannot carry an unpaid course.
do: **Request written hours** and a retirement contribution statement starting now.
**Take belt-inspection training** after thinking AI arrives only if the mine offers paid work and a place.
feel: **Alarmed** that losing half her hours could force a choice between food and heating.
S2.quote: I cannot leave mine work for an unpaid classroom.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **2028 scheduling** from possible hands-on feeder robots around 2031.
Her **training is conditional** on a real paid place; she cannot finance time away from lower mine wages.

steps.text: Request a written record of feeder hours and retirement contributions
Take paid belt-inspection training if a real place and wage are offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI by 2031 gives the office time to change schedules, and feeder robots follow around 2034. I would want the mine to say when the last human feeder shift might be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 when capable robots arrive, and I hope to have stopped working by then. A hope of retiring at 65 will not pay for food and heating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the retirement desk this month what my pension would pay at 65 and at 67. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll keep the feeder job if my health allows and the pension will not cover our basic bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried but less trapped than with two years. The extra time matters only if I can keep earning through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What pension number would let you stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pension at 65 won't pay for food and heating, I will not hand in my notice just because a robot date is on a calendar. I would ask Peter to sit with me while we add the figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown child help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grown daughter would offer help, but she has a mortgage as well. I'd rather take the feeder shift while I can than make her choose between two houses.

say: I would ask the mine for a **feeder timetable** before capable robots arrive around 2034.
I would keep working if the **pension** cannot cover our basic bills.
think: I think at **66**, I might be retired before feeder robots arrive, but the pension may be too small.
I think our **thin savings** could force me to keep shifts longer than my health wants.
do: **Ask for pension figures** at ages 65 and 67 this month.
**Keep feeder shifts** after thinking AI arrives if health permits and pension income cannot cover essentials.
feel: **Worried**, with more time to earn but no guarantee of a workable pension.
S3.quote: A hope of retiring at 65 will not pay for food and heating.
fieldNote: Her **2034 age** is 66; retirement before robots is possible but not financially settled.
She makes **continued work conditional** on health and pension adequacy, without asking her daughter to fund two homes.

steps.text: Ask the retirement desk for pension figures at 65 and 67
Keep feeder shifts if health permits and pension income falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI comes by 2036 and feeder robots around 2039, when I would be over seventy. If I can retire before then, those machines are not the main problem in my house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when thinking AI arrives, but I do not know whether my pension will cover food and heating. Peter's maintenance work may have stopped by then, so I cannot call a decade easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for the pension figures now and keep the feeder job as long as it is safe and we need the wages. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, if I'm still working, I'll compare the pension with our basic bills before deciding whether to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a little relief that robots would come so late, and a larger worry about growing old without enough money. A far-off machine cannot pay next month's groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you promise your partner a retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would like to stop at 65, but I won't promise Peter a date until we see the figures. I can tell my grown children the truth without asking them to carry us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the feeder becomes too hard physically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my body cannot manage the feeder, I would ask the mine about lighter paid work before giving up entirely. There may be no place, so I won't put it in the family budget yet.

say: I would expect **2039 feeder robots** to arrive after my hoped-for retirement.
I would still ask for **pension figures** before telling my family when I can stop.
think: I think at **68** when thinking AI arrives, I may still need wages if the pension is too small.
I think Peter’s work might end, and **thin savings** leave little room for an easy exit.
do: **Keep working** safely while wages are needed, then compare pension income with basic bills after thinking AI arrives.
**Ask** about lighter paid work if the feeder becomes too hard before retirement.
feel: **Relieved** by the late robot date, but worried about ordinary retirement income.
S4.quote: A far-off machine cannot pay next month's groceries.
fieldNote: Her **2036 age** is 68 and robot arrival around 2039 would put her at 71.
Her **income worry** persists even if robots arrive after retirement; she will only stop when pension and bills allow.

steps.text: Keep feeder shifts while safe and needed for household bills
Compare pension income with basic bills after thinking AI arrives
Ask the mine for lighter paid work if the feeder becomes unsafe

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because shifts might go before capable feeder robots arrive around 2031, and we have almost no savings. Paid inspection training with a real place would help, as would a clear pension statement I can plan around.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I came late to mine work by choice. I took this feeder job after the laundry closed, and I would rather be paid for a shift than have my children cover our groceries.

headlineQuote: I took this feeder job after the laundry closed, and I would rather be paid for a shift than have my children cover our groceries.
portrait: **Olga Mensah**, 58, is a junior feeder operator at a large limestone mine after a laundry job ended.
She has **secondary schooling**, lower mine pay, irregular household income and less than one month of expenses saved.
She avoids **AI tools** and prefers familiar work, but knows planning software could alter shifts before feeder robots arrive.
Her **retirement date** depends on pension figures and health; even a late robot date does not settle household bills.
She would take **paid inspection training** only with an actual place and wage, while protecting her grown children from her costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because feeder shifts could disappear before capable robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **real paid training place** and clear pension figures would let her plan without relying on grown children.
